```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_eipack <- requireNamespace("eiPack", quietly = TRUE)
has_eco <- requireNamespace("eco", quietly = TRUE)
library(eiPartialID)
```

Version 0.2.0 added `eiBounds()`, which extends the 2 x 2 method of Jiang,
King, Schmaltz and Tanner (2019) to R x C tables, to units nested in groups
(e.g. polls within ridings, precincts within counties), and to a ladder of
assumptions running from Duncan–Davis bounds (no model) to Goodman constancy.
The derivations, proofs and simulations are in `docs/extension/` of the source
repository. `PLAIN_LANGUAGE_GUIDE.md` there explains every rung in plain terms.
Version 0.3.0 adds signs on mean associations and contextual reinforcement
(experimental; see below), a rank guard for the projection intervals and a
bootstrap pooling test; `NEWS.md` lists the changes.

## What is reported

For each target (by default every row-by-column cell), `eiBounds()` reports:

* `estimate`: the estimated (outer) identified set for the *model-implied
  rate*. It is sharp relative to the regression function, not to the full
  data. It is not a confidence interval, and it tends to be too narrow when
  there are many noisy constraints.
* `ci_model`: a confidence interval for the model-implied rate at the observed
  compositions (the "behavioural" rate).
* `ci_actual`: a confidence interval for the *actual* rate in these units.
  It includes an allowance for unit-level deviations, which can never be
  estimated. That allowance is bounded by the Bhatia–Davis inequality (the
  default) or by the Popoviciu bound of 1/4 used by Jiang et al.
* `duncan_davis`: the model-free bounds for the actual rate.

The default confidence intervals use intersection-bound inference (Chernozhukov,
Lee and Rosen 2013). The candidate endpoints are collected by simulation, so the
interval as implemented is *algorithmic*: its coverage is supported by
simulation but not proved. Alongside it, `proj_model` and `proj_actual` give
projection intervals built from the same candidates. These have an asymptotic
guarantee for a fixed-dimensional regression with a nonsingular estimated
covariance matrix (M0 in any full-rank design; grouped models with few, large
groups) and are usually only slightly wider. If the covariance matrix is
numerically singular, candidates that use its null directions are dropped (the
interval stays valid and gets wider) and a note says so. The unit-level
allowance in `proj_actual` uses a variance bound taken from a projection
interval, so the projection columns rest only on the proved result.
`ci = "conservative"` gives the other proved interval. Jiang et al.'s CI_x
intervals are also available (`jkst = TRUE`).

Inference is conditional on the observed compositions and on the group effects.
Units are assumed independent given them, and no clustered variance is used.
A shock shared by the units of a group belongs in the mean: use M1 or M2. With
groups, `eiBounds()` also reports a pooling test of M0 against M1 (all group
shifts zero) and the test of M1's testable part against M2. The pooling test's
p-value comes from a restricted wild bootstrap: the chi-squared version
over-rejects when there are many groups (9% at a nominal 5% with 38
restrictions in the Phase 3 Monte Carlo).

## Two-by-two: the original method

```{r census, eval = has_eco}
library(eiPartialID)
data(census, package = "eco")
fit <- eiBounds(x = census$X, t = census$Y, n = census$N, model = "M0",
                targets = list(black_literate = c(1, 1)), jkst = TRUE, seed = 1)
fit
```

With `range_offset = 1e-5` and `vcov = "HC1"`, the plug-in bound and the
CI_x intervals coincide with `generateBounds()` and `evaluateBounds()`.

## Three ways to give the data

```{r interfaces, eval = has_eipack}
library(eiPack)
data(senc)                       # NC registration by race, with true cell counts
senc2 <- transform(senc, black = black + natam)   # merge a very small group
# 1. formula with counts
f1 <- eiBounds(cbind(dem, rep, non) ~ cbind(white, black), data = senc2,
               targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")), seed = 1)
# 2. data plus column names
f2 <- eiBounds(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"), cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"),
               targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")), seed = 1)
# 3. shares and sizes
X <- as.matrix(senc2[, c("white", "black")]) / senc2$total
T <- as.matrix(senc2[, c("dem", "rep", "non")]) / senc2$total
f3 <- eiBounds(x = X, t = T, n = senc2$total, targets = list(white_dem = c(1, 1)), seed = 1)
rbind(f1$table$estimate_lower, f2$table$estimate_lower, f3$table$estimate_lower)
```

Row and column totals must describe the same population. If they differ,
`eiBounds()` stops; `mismatch = "rescale"` overrides this, with a warning.

## The ladder

`ladder()` runs the rungs from the most to the least plausible:

| Rung | Assumption |
|---|---|
| DD | none |
| M2 | each group has its own linear contextual effects |
| M1(delta) | contextual effects shared, each group within `delta` of them |
| M1 | contextual effects shared; groups differ only in baselines ("group dummies") |
| L4 | as M1, and one chosen row has no contextual effect |
| L5 | constancy within each group (Goodman within groups) |
| L6 | Goodman constancy |

M0 (pooled, no groups) is reported alongside; it is not nested with the others.

```{r ladder, eval = has_eipack}
L <- ladder(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"), cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"),
            group = "county", targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")),
            row_constant = "black")
L
# truth
with(senc, sum(whdem) / sum(white))
```

## Composition range

The bounds come from requiring the implied rates to be valid probabilities at
the corners of the composition range. The choices are:

* `range = "hull"` (default): the observed units. Each group uses its own units.
* `range = "trim"`: drop extreme units from the corners (`trim = list(quantile
  = 0.01)`, `min_n = ...` or `drop = ...`). Trimmed units enter the actual rate
  only through their Duncan–Davis bounds, so trimming never relies on the model
  for them.
* `range = "extrapolate"`: impose the model beyond the data (`"simplex"` means
  pure units). This gives narrower bounds, but it is untestable, and a warning is
  printed.

## Additional restrictions

All of these keep the bounds as linear programs.

```{r restrictions, eval = has_eipack}
r <- list(
  order = list(c(high = "black", low = "white", col = "dem")),  # same composition: black >= white
  sign = list(list(row = "white", col = "dem", from = "white", to = "black", sign = 1)),
  slope = 0.5,                                                  # no rate moves > 0.5 across compositions
  external = list(list(target = c("white", "dem"), lower = 0.40, upper = 0.55))  # e.g. a survey
)
eiBounds(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"), cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"),
         targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")), restrictions = r, seed = 1)
```

`zeros` fixes structural zeros, e.g. a party that did not run. `linear` takes
any linear restriction on the contextual-effect matrices.

## Signs on associations and contextual reinforcement

**Status: experimental in 0.3.0.** The M-SIGN module is under revision after
two referee reports (`docs/extension/reviews/B_PI_RESPONSE_PLAN.md`), and
`print()` flags it. Two kinds of "monotone EI" belief (Elzayn et al.,
*Monotone Ecological Inference*) can be added to the linear-contextual-effects
rungs as extra rows:

* the **between** association $\delta_B$: within the same unit, group $r$ is
  on average more (or less) likely than the rest to choose column $c$. It is a
  weighted average over units with weights $N_i x_{ir}(1 - x_{ir})$, so pure
  units get no weight and one large mixed unit can dominate; it is not an
  ordering in every unit;
* the **within** (contextual) association $\delta_W$: with the default
  one-vs-rest version (`"W1"`), the rates of group $r$, and of everyone else,
  rise (or fall) on average with **group $r$'s share** of the unit (the
  predictor is $r$'s share in both parts). With `"W2"`, $\Delta_r$ is the
  within-group association of every original group with $r$'s share,
  **pooled into one sum**: its sign does not sign each group's association
  (W1 and W2 can even have opposite signs while every group's rate rises).
  A direction for each named group separately needs separate restrictions,
  which are not yet available;
* **contextual reinforcement (CR)**: $\delta_B$ and $\delta_W$ have the same
  sign, without saying which.

All three are model-implied means with design weights $N_i$. A sign is one
linear row; CR is a union of two branches. With the one-vs-rest version (`"W1"`,
the default, and every 2 x 2 table) CR is a single slab
$D^r \in \operatorname{hull}\{\gamma_r ER^r, ER^r\}$ (the order of the two
ends depends on the sign of $ER^r$), so it stays one LP. The other pairings
(`"W2"`, `"pair"`) can give **disjoint intervals**; every piece is printed,
`[a, b] U [c, d]` (use `union = "hull"` for the hull). The `*_gap_*` columns of
`fit$table` keep only the widest gap; `fit$pieces` has every piece.

Under grouped rungs (M1, M1(delta), M2, L4 with groups) a sign is **one pooled
restriction across groups**, not one per group; the rows are the correct
district functionals, but sharpness is proved only for the pooled model M0, and
a note says so at fit time.

```{r sign}
set.seed(2)
n <- 200
x <- pmin(pmax(rbeta(n, 2, 2) * 0.8 + 0.1, 0.02), 0.98)
m0 <- 0.40 + 0.20 * x; m1 <- 0.55 + 0.05 * x          # linear means, CR holds
t <- (1 - x) * rbeta(n, m0 * 15, (1 - m0) * 15) + x * rbeta(n, m1 * 15, (1 - m1) * 15)
N <- sample(300:3000, n, replace = TRUE)
gap <- list(gap = matrix(c(1, -1, 0, 0), 2, 2))      # B(X -> T) - B(notX -> T)
jkst <- eiBounds(x = x, t = t, n = N, targets = gap, seed = 1)   # linear rung alone
jkst$table[, c("estimate_lower", "estimate_upper", "ci_model_lower", "ci_model_upper")]
cr <- eiBounds(x = x, t = t, n = N, targets = gap, seed = 1,
               restrictions = list(cr = list(list(row = 1, col = 1))))
cr
dW <- eiBounds(x = x, t = t, n = N, targets = gap, seed = 1,
               restrictions = list(assoc = list(list(type = "dW", row = 1, col = 1, sign = 1))))
dW$table[, c("estimate_lower", "estimate_upper", "ci_model_lower", "ci_model_upper")]
```

`eiRedundancy()` (stored in `$sign` when sign or CR restrictions are given)
reports, for each restriction and target, whether it is already implied by the
data and the rung, cuts the set but not this quantity, or narrows this
quantity, with the gain when added first and when added last. The verdict uses
a face test (one LP per endpoint), never solver dual values. It also shows the
associations' intervals under the rung alone and the EGGHM quantities
$\widehat{ER}$, $\widehat{NM} = \gamma\widehat{ER}$ and $\gamma$:

```{r sign2}
cr$sign$descriptive
cr$sign$verdicts[, c("restriction", "verdict_first", "gain_first")]
```

How to read and report these:

* **Report the rung alone beside the belief.** When restrictions are given,
  `print()` shows the rung-only estimate and CIs (`base_*` columns) next to
  the restricted result, so the price of the belief is visible.
* **What the estimate is.** For M0, the estimate is the estimated bound, given
  the fitted regression and the design, for the model-implied quantity
  (PHASE5a R3(b)); it is sharp relative to the regression, not to the full
  joint distribution, which can be smaller. Under grouped rungs it is an outer
  set.
* **What the data can and cannot check.** A sign on $\delta_W$ can be refuted
  by aggregate data. A sign on $\delta_B$ and CR are always feasible only in
  the model-free problem with continuous unit tables (Duncan–Davis margins, no
  linear rung, no other restriction). With the linear rung they can be
  rejected jointly with it, and with integer counts, known cells or other
  restrictions CR can be refuted outright. An empty plug-in set is a sample
  diagnostic; the emptiness test is the level-controlled rejection; the notes
  say whether the rung alone is rejected. A rejection of the combination is
  not evidence that the belief holds.
* **What they can buy, and the price.** In the PHASE5a Monte Carlo (2 x 2,
  truth on the CR edge) the **conservative** CR interval had median width
  0.36 against 1.1 for the linear rung alone, with coverage 0.99. The default
  CR interval is the CLR branch union, which is **algorithmic** (coverage
  supported by simulation, not proved); `print()` shows the projection
  interval beside it. If CR is false, the interval stays narrow, non-empty and
  wrong: in the referee's experiment at 600 units it covered 0 of 400 times
  under a moderate departure, while the linear rung alone covered every time.
* **Never intersect the estimated bracket
  $\operatorname{hull}\{\gamma\widehat{ER}, \widehat{ER}\}$ with a confidence
  interval.** Treating the estimated bracket as known under-covers at the CR
  edge, and the failure does not go away as $n$ grows (the 8–10% miss rates
  in PHASE5a are for its design). The package inflates every piece instead:
  the conservative CI inflates each piece of the slab before taking the
  maximum; the CLR CI takes the union of the two branch CIs, each at the full
  level.
* **"Cuts the set, not this target"** means zero gain for this target; it
  does not mean the restriction is implied (it may narrow other targets).
* **Weight concentration.** `fit$sign$concentration` gives, for each signed
  association, the largest unit weight and the effective number of units.
* Our $\widehat{ER}$ uses the fitted $E[T \mid X]$; it equals the EGGHM
  $T$-based $\widehat{ER}$ when `weights = "n"`. In the "descriptive only"
  table, $\widehat{ER}$ is the weighted aggregate regression slope and
  $\widehat{NM}=\gamma\widehat{ER}$ the neighbourhood-model gap, for the named
  focal group; neither is imposed. The `voter_vax` agreement is an arithmetic
  check, not a validation of the beliefs.

**Reading the output.**

* The estimate is a set and the confidence interval is a different object;
  read them on separate lines. When there are several pieces, values in a gap
  between estimated pieces are excluded by the assumptions, but a confidence
  interval may still cover them. The pieces carry no probability weights, and
  the hull (`union = "hull"`) includes the gaps.
* **What a sign does not mean.** A sign on $\delta_W$ is a statement about a
  weighted average over units. It does not say that every precinct, every
  district, or every rival group satisfies the direction, and it is not an
  ordering at every composition. Within-unit covariances also reflect sorting
  of voters across precincts, campaign targeting and other differences between
  precincts, so a causal reading ("neighbours change how people vote") needs
  a separate design. A sign that the rung already implies (see the "already
  implied" table) adds nothing.
* **Columns and orientation.** Restrictions on several columns must respect
  that the columns add to one: a sign on "yes" is the opposite sign on "no" in
  a two-column table, and a 2 × 3 table (two groups, three outcomes) is not the
  same problem as a 3 × 2 table. "Both signs" in the ladder means both weakly
  positive or both weakly negative.
* **Turnout.** If abstention is a column, the eligible population is the
  denominator. Loyalty among those who voted can then coexist with a negative
  gap in the eligible-population rate, so state which denominator a belief is
  about.
* **Other methods.** King's EI and hierarchical R × C models produce point
  estimates with posterior intervals. A posterior mean that falls inside a
  sign bound is not independent support for the sign, since both rest on the
  same aggregates. The useful check is a benchmark with known truth
  (aggregated individual-level panels or linked surveys), with the sign
  choices fixed in advance on other units.

`ladder()` takes sign and CR rungs through `sign_rungs`, e.g.
`sign_rungs = list("M0 + CR" = list(restrictions = list(cr = list(list(row = 1, col = 1)))))`.

## Sensitivity and breakdown

```{r sens, eval = has_eco}
sv <- sensitivity(fit, eta = c(0, 0.02, 0.05))
sv[, c("eta", "estimate_lower", "estimate_upper")]
breakdown(fit, "black_literate", threshold = 0.5, which = "ci_model")
```

`eta` is how far average rates may depart from straight lines, in probability
units, in ways the data cannot detect. The breakdown value is the largest
`eta` at which the conclusion ("the rate is above 0.5") still holds.

## Benchmarks

`eiBenchmark()` runs the rungs on datasets with known cell counts, and reports
whether each interval contains the truth and how wide it is.

```{r bench, eval = has_eipack}
truth <- with(senc, matrix(c(sum(whdem), sum(whrep), sum(whnon),
                             sum(bldem + natamdem), sum(blrep + natamrep), sum(blnon + natamnon)),
                           2, 3, byrow = TRUE))
b <- eiBenchmark(list(senc = list(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"),
                                  cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"), group = "county", truth = truth)),
                 rungs = c("M0", "M1", "L5"), seed = 1)
aggregate(cbind(in_ci_actual, width_ci_actual, width_dd) ~ rung, b, mean)
```

### Real elections with known truth: ei.Datasets

`eiDatasetsTables()` builds 492 tables with exact truth from the New Zealand
general elections 2002–2020 in the `ei.Datasets` package. In each electorate,
polling places are the units, party votes are the rows and electorate
(candidate) votes are the columns. The repository's
`benchmarks/run_ei_datasets_benchmark.R` runs the full benchmark, and the
results are stored in `benchmarks/results/`.

```{r eidatasets, eval = FALSE}
tb <- eiDatasetsTables(elections = 2020)
eiBenchmark(tb[1:5], rungs = c("M0", "L6"), seed = 1)
```
